10 ANNEX – AFUDC ( BONBRIGHT)

AFUDC Versus CWIP Two Methods, FERC and other jurisdictions recognize that there are two alternate regulatory practices by which these carrying charges of debt interest and reasonable equity return on construction capital are recovered in rates. One method capitalizes the carrying charges incurred during the construction period as allowance for funds used during construction (AFUDC). AFUDC is recorded part as current income, part as an offset to interest expenses, but no cash payments are made by ratepayers during construction. The payments from ratepayers to recover the carrying charges begin when the completed plant goes on stream. The entire cost of the plant (including AFUDC) is added to rate base, and it earns a rate of return on investment and is depreciated over the life of that plant. The second method is to include construction work in progress (CWIP) in the rate base. (CWIP includes accrued AFUDC on investment not in rate base.) The regulatee recovers its carrying charges currently from ratepayers through the return component of its rates, rather than adding them to the cost of construction for recovery when the plant is in service. The return on CWIP is recorded as income on a current basis (like AFUDC), and actual cash payments are made by the ratepayers currently (unlike AFUDC). Although each method is intended to provide an opportunity to recover the carrying charges, they differ primarily according to when the investment is permitted in rate base, i.e., when the carrying charges are reflected in the cost of service and thus in rates charged to ratepayers. The courts generally defer to the regulatory agency's choice of methods. In a rate base measured by original cost, there would be no occasion for an allowance for funds used during construction if capital devoted by the company to the public service were given an opportunity to enjoy a fair rate of return from the very moment of its investment. Some commissions have granted this opportunity by including directly in the rate base amounts expended on work still under construction, CWIP, and hence not yet rendering public service. Historically, it was felt that unless these CWIP amounts were relatively small compared to the investments in completed plant- which for recent nuclear plants they most certainly are not- their immediate inclusion in the rate base would be a departure from the general principle that the public utility consumers in any given year should pay a return only on the cost of those assets that are performing for them a useful service. In any event, the general practice historically was to withhold from the rate base major plant construction costs until the plant itself has become part of the "used and useful" property.

As long as this withholding practice existed, there arose a need for some ratemaking provision whereby the company might eventually receive an adequate compensation for its advance commitment of capital. The standard provision of this nature, and the one that traditionally was believed to be most satisfactory, at least as long as the company could maintain its financial integrity, and except in circumstances where the stability and predictability of rates and revenues became a major issue, was that of a computed allowance for funds used during construction, or AFUDC as it is commonly known. However, this allowance should not be restricted to the interest on debentures, if any, that the company may pay on loans designed to finance the construction work, but should also include a fair return on the equity capital required to support the debt instruments.

So far as we know, the propriety of some allowance of this type as a component of the rate base has been conceded by all commissions. But, the standard was once challenged by the FPC, which insisted that the allowed rate of interest should be limited to the low contract rates payable on borrowed funds instead of being set at rates, typical of the usual fair rate of return. The staff even intimated that, on grounds of accounting principles, the compensation payable to companies for their commitment of capital in advance of any claim to a fair return should take the form of later enhancements in the allowed rate of return instead of taking the form of enhancements in the rate base. The relevant accounting principles were found to lie in the strict adherence of orthodox fixed-asset accounting to the principle of cost. While the failure of a company to earn any return on capital embodied in work in progress was conceded to justify more liberal later allowances of opportunities to make a profit, it was held not to constitute a "cost" in an accurate sense, at least not in any sense recognized in financial accounting. This attempt by the Commission's experts to judge the merits of a practical rule of rate control by an appeal to "generally acceptable principles of accounting" gave some representatives for the utility companies a dose of their own medicine. We refer particularly to attempts by expert witnesses for public utility companies to invoke "generally accepted principles of accounting" in support of the recognition of "acquisition costs" rather than of "aboriginal costs" as components of the rate base. Both sides in rate-case disputes have a tendency to find these "accepted principles" relevant when, but only when, they comport with whatever rules of ratemaking they favor in the case at bar.

In 1971 the FPC started using the term "allowance for funds used during construction" instead of "interest during construction" on its accounting system (its Uniform System of Accounts began January 1, 1937). The Commission developed a formula for the maximum AFUDC that includes both the net cost of borrowed funds used for construction and a reasonable rate on other funds when so used (Johnson, 1977). According to Phillips (1984, p. 323): Under the formula, the embedded book-cost rates for the prior year are used for debt and preferred stock, while the cost rate for common equity "shall be the rate granted common equity in the last rate proceeding before the ratemaking body having primary rate jurisdiction. If such cost rate is not available, the average rate actually earned during the preceding three years shall be used." Further, since 1977, AFUDC has been segregated into two component parts borrowed funds and other funds. The former have been assigned to the "interest charges" section of the income statement; the latter remain in the "other income and deductions" section.

FPC Order No. 561 (1977): AFUDC. In February 1977, the FPC issued Order 561 establishing a uniform formulary method of determining the maximum rates to be used in computing AFUDC. The primary objective of the order was to establish a method which would give recognition to the interrelationship between capital utilized for rate case purposes and the capital components of AFUDC in a manner which would permit a utility to achieve a rate of return on its total utility operations at approximately the rate which would be allowed in a rate case. Order 561 established a uniform formula method of determining the maximum allowable AFUDC rate. The formula assumes that short-term debt is the first source of funds for construction, with the remainder financed from long-term debt, preferred stock and common equity. The embedded book cost rates are used for debt and preferred stock, while the rate allowed in the last primary rate proceeding is used for common equity. The FPC order also provided for semi-annual compounding of AFUDC. The primary purpose of AFUDC is to capitalize the costs of financing construction, separate the effects of the construction program from current operations, and to allocate current capital costs to future periods when these capital facilities are producing revenue. FPC Order No. 561 has been adopted by most state regulatory commissions as the method for computing AFUDC.

The Commission's original position seems quite unconvincing, since it had little or no bearing on the question of whether the provisions for compensation on capital that was tied up in work under construction should take the form of a rate-base enhancement or of a rate-of-return enhancement. Here, we think standard procedure is wise in accepting the former alternative, and for reasons quite apart from the academic question whether the AFUDC---called "phantom income" by Business Week (1980) and "funny money"-- by others is regarded as a recordation of an actual cost or, alternatively, as the allowance of a credit to the corporation for temporary denial of opportunity to earn a return on cost.

However, in our opinion, the latter interpretation is correct, since a failure to earn any return on the cost of a capital asset is not in itself a cost in a strict sense. As to the proposal to disallow rate-base enhancements in favor of a more liberal fair rate of return, this would impose upon those people who must calculate the proper percentage rate the obligation of attempting to do indirectly, and without benefit of adequate accounting data, what the overt allowances for funds used during construction do directly and systematically. Anyone who has faced the difficult problem of establishing a fair rate of return or of estimating the cost of capital can hardly welcome a change in the rules of rate-base determination that would needlessly add to their difficulties.

As to the question whether the AFUDC should be based on percentage rates approximating contract interest on secure loans, or whether it should be based on a higher rate approximating an accepted fair rate of return, the answer should depend on the answer to the further question: "Which rate comes closer to reflecting the time discount that the investment market places on investments on which the anticipated return is subject to a material delay, as compared to investments that promise immediate income?" The well-recognized market preference for early, and hence less uncertain, realization strongly suggests the allowance of a time discount not lower than that reflected by a standard fair rate of return. There is no question of the growing and grave importance of AFUDC. Makhija and Thompson (1986) show that AFUDC as a percent of net income for Moody's 24 utilities went from only 7.8 percent in 1967 to 51.4 percent in 1983 (with a high of 51.6 percent in 1982).

Controversy: Howe and Rasmussen (1982, p. 92) summarize the present sound and fury surrounding how company funds committed prior to a plant going on stream should be handled: One of the more controversial rate-base issues has been whether or not to include construction work in progress in the rate base. Construction work in progress (or CWIP) is the investment in plant under construction. Its inclusion can lead to a mismatch of rate base with revenues and expenses and to the inclusion of property not used and useful in the rate base. Some jurisdictions have included CWIP in rate bases. Others follow more traditional ratemaking and do not include CWIP. The allowance for funds used during construction has been developed to permit the capital costs the utility has during the construction period to be compensated by the future consumer actually to be served by the plant under construction. The cost of capital used in financing the construction is capitalized, i.e., the original cost of the plant recorded on the utility's books includes capital charges and other overheads, The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission provides in its uniform system of accounts that the costs of short-term debt should be applied to construction first. If the short-term debt is not sufficient to cover the amount of construction work in progress, the weighted cost of long-term financing is then applied to the remaining amount of construction.

The use of an allowance for funds used during construction is less costly than is construction work in progress. An allowance for funds used during construction does not produce taxable income to the utility. Rather, the taxable income results in higher book depreciation charges and more earnings in later years when the plant is used and useful. Allowing a return on construction work in progress does create taxable income, on the other hand. As a result, $1 of equity return earned on construction work in progress increases the cost of service by $2. A tax deferral accompanies the allowance for funds used during construction, which makes this method of recovering capital costs during construction less costly than the inclusion of construction work in progress in the rate base.

Despite one's position on the dispute on CWIP versus AFUDC, it is apparent that because of the hard times confronting utilities in the 1980s---involving significant cash flow, earnings, and coverage ratio problems---many state and federal commissions began to allow part or all of CWIP in the rate base in varying amounts and under varying conditions (see Phillips, 1984, pp. 324-325 for details). The decision whether to include CWIP in the rate base becomes very crucial when a commission decides to cancel a plant. If CWIP is not allowed in the rate base, consistency calls for not including the amortized balance in the rate base (Urban, 1984). If CWIP were allowed in the rate base, consistency suggests inclusion of the unamortized balance as well. Also, commissions differ on the treatment of AFUIDC. A remedy for plant cancellation that is more favorable to the utility (ratepayer) would include a short (long) CWIP amortization period, inclusion (exclusion) of the unamortized portion of CWIP in the rate base, and inclusion (disallowance) of AFUDC in the rate base.

It is an unsettled issue in public utilities whether CWIP in the rate base is preferred although Morin (1986) presents a lucid case for CWIP inclusion based on a simulation model. He finds that CWIP inclusion benefits ratepayers by lowering the costs of both debt and equity capital and by lowering rates over the lifetime of the plant as the rate base is not permanently enhanced by the amount of financing costs accrued during construction.

On the other hand, Makhija and Thompson (1986) found ratepayers may prefer either approach. When the AFUDC rate is large and growth is slow, the ratepayer will prefer CWIP in the rate base. As growth decreases, the benefits of CWIP decline. The shareholders prefer CWIP if the AFUDC rate is low and growth is rapid. When the AFUDC rate is intermediate somewhere between large and small, the shareholders and ratepayers both may prefer AFUDC regulation. They believe that if there are any benefits to ratepayers from CWIP, it is from reduced revenue requests. Because many states set an arbitrary rate in calculating AFUDC that is far below the cost of capital, investors (ratepayers) prefer (don't prefer) CWIP in the rate base. In their opinion, most of the reason people want CWIP in the rate base is because the AFUDC rate is too low and it is politically easier to get increased earnings from CWIP inclusion than from rate increases. The conditions for inclusion and the amounts allowed for CWIP in the rate base vary considerably by jurisdiction. As of 1978, 34 state regulatory commissions allowed CWIP under both broad and narrow (as was true of FERC) conditions (Muhs & Schauer, 1980). The number of inclusion states has increased rapidly in recent years.

FERC Order No. 298 (1983): CWIP. The FERC's historic policy regarding CWIP generally prohibited inclusion of CWIP in rate base until the facility became "used and useful." In 1976, the FPC promulgated regulations (Order 555) that provided three exceptions: (1) for construction of pollution control facilities; (2) for construction of fuel conversion facilities; and (3) for certain other situations where the utility is in severe financial difficulty which could not otherwise be alleviated without materially increasing the cost of electricity to consumers. On May 16, 1983, the FERC issued new regulations on the treatment of FERC jurisdictional CWIP (Order No. 298). Order 298 permits any public utility regulated by the FERC to file to include in rate base up to 50 percent of jurisdictionally allowable CWIP. This would be subject to a two-year impact limitation of 6 percent per year on the wholesale rate increase attributable to the inclusion of CWIP Order 298 supplements existing regulations which provide for inclusion in rate base of 100 percent of jurisdictionally allowable CWIP associated with pollution control and fuel conversion facilities.

Order 298 results in the use of both CWIP in rate base and AFUDC. CWIP costs not put in the rate base are given AFUDC treatment. It also provides that public utilities are eligible to file to include CWIP in rate base irrespective of their financial condition. The regulations contain new filing requirements that will enable the FERC to evaluate the prudence of the claimed costs, including the extent to which the investment is a part of a least cost power supply strategy. They also allow wholesale customers to escape liability for CWIP if they can prove that they bear no responsibility for the decision to build a new plant and will, in fact, purchase no full or partial firm power requirements which involve the new plant. These regulations cover only the share of the facility which is to provide FERC jurisdictional power. The regulations do not directly affect how state public utility commissions elect to treat state jurisdictional CWIP. Some states such as Wisconsin, allow some CWIP and allow some AFUDC on the proportion of CWIP not allowed in the rate base. FERC has given this mixed approach some consideration.

Two sharply divergent views of the electric utility industry emerged from the comments concerning Order 298. According to privately owned utility companies, the industry has been (and remains) in difficult financial straits, which raises serious questions as to the industry's ability to finance today the construction of electrical generation capacity which will be needed later this decade and beyond. Under this view, utilities' inability to earn their allowed rate of return reduces current cash flow, tending to increase the need for additional external financing. This tends in turn to increase risk and thereby to increase the actual cost of capital. These factors then tend to jeopardize the industry's ability to finance the major new facilities which the industry forecasts are needed to replace inefficient existing facilities and to satisfy increased consumer demand.

These financial constraints are said to have caused the cancellation and deferral of substantial new capacity over the past few years. Financial concerns also have tended to bias the industry's investment in favor of smaller facilities which may require less construction capital, but which are more costly to consumers in the long run because of higher fuel and maintenance costs.

The utilities' wholesale power customers present a different view. They recognize that the utility industry has faced financial difficulties over the last few years, but say that the situation has brightened as state regulatory commissions have recognized the need for higher rates. Moreover, they claim that the extensive cancellations and deferrals of new capacity reflect a belated recognition of sharply reduced growth in electricity demand, and the utilities' inability to obtain adequate financing. The ratepayers thus oppose the inclusion of CWIP in rate base as an unnecessary and unduly costly answer to yesterday's problem. They recommend strongly against the inclusion of any CWIP in rate base.

The Commission took an intermediate view of the situation. The rule attempted to strike a balance between the competing views and takes a modest step at tying supply and demand together in a somewhat clearer fashion. The purpose of the rule is thus threefold: (1) to mitigate any bias which may discourage additional capital investment in needed facilities;

(2) to enable the need for those facilities to be more accurately evaluated by price signals which reflect today some of the costs associated with future facilities; and (3) to mitigate the sudden price increases which tend to result under an AFUDC policy thereby furthering the goal of rate stability.

The current treatment adopted by several state regulators is to not allow CWIP in rate base, but to allow accrual of AFUDC. However, in the future, many utilities may require rate base inclusion of CWIP before beginning large construction projects because of increased uncertainty over recoverability of plant costs.
